bibliography.note: Malm, J., Terzhevik, A., Bengtsson, L., Boyarinov, P., Glinsky, A., Palshin, N. & Petrov, M. 1997. Temperature and salt content regimes in three shallow ice-covered lakes: 2. Heat and mass fluxes. Nordic Hydrology 28(2): 129–152 (the journal is now Hydrology Research, the name Crossref shows; Crossref's title drops the '2. Heat and mass fluxes' part, which LUP gives).

claims.claim: early in winter heat from the sediment is the main heat source, 0.6–4.5 W m⁻² in small ice-covered lakes (with Bengtsson et al. 1996)
claims.note: Abstract only. The abstract gives the sediment-to-water heat flux as the main heat source in early and mid-winter, depth-dependent, 1–4.5 W m⁻² in early winter and 0.5–3 W m⁻² in late winter, in three small shallow ice-covered lakes. The 0.6 lower bound is not Malm et al.'s (theirs is 1 early, 0.5 late); presumably it is Bengtsson et al. 1996's.

claims.claim: lateral transport from shallow to deep water can match the vertical fluxes
claims.note: Abstract only. The abstract says heat moved from shallow regions to the deep parts during winter, 'of the same order as the vertical fluxes'.

claims.claim: under ice the bed's heat drives a down-slope current of a few mm/s (ICE_SLOPE_V 0.003 m/s)
claims.note: Abstract only, and the abstract gives no current speed; check this in the full text (it may be in part 1, doi:10.2166/nh.1997.0007, or in Bengtsson et al. 1996).

claims.claim: the bed gives off the summer's stored heat at 1–4.5 W/m²
claims.note: Abstract only. 1–4.5 W m⁻² is the abstract's EARLY-winter range; late winter is 0.5–3 W m⁻², so a constant 1–4.5 would overstate late-winter heating.
